claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and low initial dislocation density.
The initial alloy contains no secondary precipitates or phase transformations.
Uniaxial tensile loading will be applied at 500–600 °C over strain rates of approximately 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Yield strength will be nearly insensitive to strain rate at 500–600 °C.
At 500–600 °C, deformation transitions from dislocation glide to stress-assisted dislocation climb.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb is controlled by lattice diffusion.
Transient solute atmospheres or vacancies may facilitate climb over glide barriers.
Intermediate-temperature thermal activation enables dislocations to overcome obstacles by vacancy-mediated climb rather than glide.
Stress exponents greater than 5 occur during intermediate-temperature deformation.
Intermediate-temperature deformation can exhibit activation energies of approximately 268–380 kJ/mol.
Activation energies of approximately 268–380 kJ/mol correspond to lattice-diffusion-controlled deformation.
Diffusion-controlled climb makes yield stress less sensitive to imposed strain rate than athermal dislocation glide.
A stress exponent significantly above 5 indicates a diffusion-controlled deformation mechanism.
At room temperature, yield strength is highly strain-rate-sensitive because of athermal dislocation glide and forest hardening.
Dynamic recrystallization and grain-boundary precipitation can occur in the 500–600 °C range under high-stress conditions.
At cryogenic temperatures deformation is glide-dominated, whereas at very high temperatures superplasticity or grain-boundary sliding occurs.
The glide-to-climb transition temperature depends on alloy composition and initial dislocation density.
Trace impurities or surface oxides can provide alternative diffusion paths and alter strain-rate sensitivity.
A statistically significant linear increase in yield strength with strain rate would indicate glide-dominated deformation.
Activation energy outside 268–380 kJ/mol together with a stress exponent below 5 would falsify the proposed lattice-diffusion-controlled climb mechanism.
